tasks.extracted: Conclusion 18-1 (the committee's judgment: conclusive evidence): completely substituting e-cigarettes for cigarettes reduces exposure to numerous toxicants and carcinogens in cigarette smoke. The chapter's synthesis says all studies showed significantly reduced biomarkers of exposure in people who substituted e-cigarettes for cigarettes. Examples: a 5-day randomized study of 105 people (urinary biomarkers 29 to 95% lower and exhaled carbon monoxide 27 to 89% lower after partial or complete switching; people who used both products and replaced half their cigarettes had 7 to 38% reductions and 1 to 20% higher nicotine equivalents); 40 people followed for four weeks (exhaled carbon monoxide 80% lower with e-cigarettes only and 52% lower with both products; acrolein metabolite 3-HPMA 79% and 60% lower); and a cross-sectional comparison of 181 people in five groups in which long-term exclusive e-cigarette use had lower NNAL than every other group while nitrosamine and volatile-compound metabolites in people who used both products were similar to those in people who only smoked. tasks.extracted: Chapter 7, nicotine (60 studies, 5 from the UK): large variation by design, definitions, biomarker and sample type and exposure duration. Five meta-analyses (1 longitudinal, 4 cross-sectional) of nicotine and its metabolites in people who vaped and people who smoked at least weekly found no significant differences. tasks.extracted: Chapter 7 design: two review questions (effects of vaping and secondhand exposure on markers associated with the risk of health conditions; effects in people with existing conditions on disease outcomes); no study answered the second for exposure biomarkers. Comparisons were relative (against people who smoke) and absolute (against people who use no nicotine); studies varied in quality and definitions (for example grouping people who vape and smoke with exclusive vaping, or comparing occasional vaping with daily smoking). Follow-up was a single use to 7 days (acute) or 8 days to 12 months; the authors write that they were unable to summarise findings on longer-term (more than 12 months) vaping exposure, with some studies allowing too little wash-out for biomarkers with long half-lives. Meta-analyses were run wherever possible, but inconsistent designs, reporting, group definitions and exposure periods meant only a few studies could be pooled.

tasks.extracted: The authors' reading (Chapter 7, Implications): compared with smoking, vaping leads to a substantial reduction in biomarkers of toxicant exposure, but the degree of any residual risk remains unclear, mainly because people who stopped smoking long ago (with and without vaping) and people who have never smoked or vaped were rarely compared. Most studies had some methodological concerns; a lack of difference from people who use no nicotine may reflect insensitive methods, background exposures or truly similar exposure. Historical tobacco use can greatly affect many biomarkers and most people who vape previously smoked for a long time; the authors ask for strict definitions of exclusive vaping and biological checks of status. They state that many pooled findings came from tobacco industry-funded randomized trials in confinement lasting up to 7 days and call for independent research outside confinement and with longer follow-up.

tasks.source_read: GOV.UK HTML (Main findings and Summary pages; the 1,468-page report PDF was not opened)
tasks.extracted: Chapter 8, markers of potential harm (41 unique studies in 43 publications): the authors list obscuring differences (different markers; group definitions with smoking or vaping status usually not checked by a biological test; mostly acute exposures, while these markers take weeks or months to normalise after people stop smoking; confounding and few controlled studies). Oxidative stress: LDL cholesterol no difference; HDL inconsistent; 8-isoprostane mixed; limited evidence for the rest. Inflammation: pooled data from 3 cross-sectional studies showed C-reactive protein lower than in people who smoke and similar to people who use no nicotine, and lower sICAM-1 than in people who smoke, but controlled and longitudinal studies did not confirm this; no definite conclusion. Endothelial function (none pooled): acute vaping (with or without nicotine) and acute smoking each reduced flow-mediated dilation in the short term; a single randomized trial found that 4 weeks of switching from smoking to vaping improved it; no controlled study compared people who vape with people who use no nicotine. Platelet activation (4 studies): no conclusions. The authors' summary: acute vaping might cause endothelial dysfunction as much as acute smoking but switching might improve endothelial function in the longer term. Their implications: research on these markers is at an early stage, most studies cannot inform the medium or long term, and studies of people who vape and have never smoked are needed.

tasks.extracted: Chapter 11, cardiovascular markers (41 studies, 27 of them cross-over or acute-exposure designs; mixed quality; no longer-term summary possible). Heart rate (31 studies, 9 pooled): acutely, vaping raised heart rate less than smoking; in longer-term comparisons heart rate was lower in people who vape than in people who smoke when the groups were mutually exclusive. Blood pressure (30 studies, 9 pooled in 10 meta-analyses): cross-sectional meta-analyses of people with at least 3 months or a year of vaping found lower blood pressure than in people who smoke and no difference from people who use no nicotine (the authors presume most had stopped smoking). Pulse wave velocity (9 studies, none pooled): may fall after a sustained switch, but the longest follow-up was 4 months; it rose after acute nicotine vaping but not non-nicotine vaping. One randomized trial found that switching improved flow-mediated dilation after one month.

tasks.extracted: Exposure was recorded at the first wave only; former use means ever use, even 1 or 2 puffs, and not now; current use means every day or some days; retention 83.2% (Wave 2), 78.4% (Wave 3), 73.5% (Wave 4). Outcomes were self-reported physician diagnoses in the past 12 months. Authors' stated limits: self-reported exposure and diagnoses; observational data with relatively short follow-up, so causality could not be established; no time-varying exposure or confounding; device characteristics unavailable; lung function not measured. They also describe reverse causation (people with early symptoms switching to e-cigarettes or quitting) as a bias that could hide an association.

tasks.extracted: Chapter 11 (cardiovascular): as in 2018, to date there is still no available evidence on whether vaping is associated with clinical cardiovascular outcomes (coronary heart disease, stroke, peripheral arterial disease) or subclinical atherosclerosis. Overall, the extent to which vaping presents a risk for cardiovascular health remains uncertain, though the authors expect the risk to be much less than that of cigarette smoking based on the toxicant profile. 27 of the 41 included studies were cross-over or acute-exposure designs that cannot answer questions about cardiovascular health outcomes; the authors call for studies comparing rates of coronary heart disease, peripheral arterial disease and stroke between people who use no nicotine, people who use tobacco and people who vape. No study was found in people with an existing cardiovascular condition. Animal studies (16) suggest possible long-term changes; no human evidence.

tasks.extracted: Chapter 10 (respiratory; 25 studies, no meta-analyses): the authors conclude there is insufficient evidence from spirometry, exhaled nitric oxide, impulse oscillometry, bronchoscopy and imaging on whether vaping affects lung function after acute, short-to-medium or long-term exposure; imaging and bronchoscopy studies were very short-term or confounded by tobacco or cannabis smoking in the vaping groups. Asthma (4 small studies): limited evidence that vaping negatively affects lung function among adults with asthma, and differences in designs, diagnoses and measurements prevent any conclusions. COPD: two articles from the same group of patients reported improvements in some spirometry measures in the group that used vaping products compared with baseline and none in the group that smoked; the authors conclude limited evidence for fewer exacerbations in adults who smoke, have COPD and switch completely, for up to 5 years. Cell and animal studies (47 in vitro, 25 animal): aerosol may cause airway adverse effects in these models. The authors say studies of long-term vaping are urgently needed and that it is not clear whether the spirometry changes are large enough to matter clinically.

tasks.extracted: Chapter 9 (cancer): the National Academies found no available evidence on whether vaping is associated with cancer risk and the Committee on Toxicity found existing evidence insufficient; this review calls the human literature growing but still modest. Biomarkers of exposure to several carcinogens are lower in people who vape than in people who smoke (the authors call this conclusive evidence of lower exposure); inflammation and oxidative stress findings show no systematic relationship and are insufficient to draw conclusions; gene expression and DNA methylation studies (8, none from the UK) are limited by missing smoking comparison groups; no study assessed people with an existing or previous cancer; cell and animal studies are hard to translate. The authors state that biomarker studies need longer follow-up to show whether vaping reduces cancer risk compared with smoking. No cancer incidence data are presented.

tasks.extracted: Scope and cut-off (Chapters 2, 7, 11 and 16): the authors conducted two systematic reviews (health risks of vaping; harm perceptions); for the health chapters they first summarised the 2018 Public Health England review, the National Academies 2018 report and the Committee on Toxicity report, then their own review, using an algorithm to decide on meta-analyses (Table 6 of Chapter 2 of the full report, not seen). Their two review protocol questions concern (1) the effect of vaping and secondhand exposure on markers associated with the risk of health conditions and (2) the effects of vaping among people with existing health conditions on disease outcomes; for cardiovascular disease and for exposure markers no study addressed the second. The search cut-off for the health chapters was July 2021, and the authors note that new studies have since been published and recommend continual updating. Databases, search terms, screening and risk-of-bias tool are not named on the pages read.

Discussion › Limitations: people who have never smoked are the most reliable group in which to estimate effects of e-cigarettes, people who neither smoke nor use e-cigarettes should be the main comparison group, adjustment is unlikely to fully remove confounding between e-cigarette use and smoking, and comparisons with smoking do not permit reliable ascertainment of the direct health impact of e-cigarettes.
